# Abstract

Between the proclamation of the Republic of Turkey in October 1923 and 2026AD, the population within the state's modern 779.608 km² polygonal territory multiplied more than sixfold, expanding from 13,1M at independence to 13,65M in the first general census of 1927AD, 20,95M in 1950AD, 35,61M in 1970AD, 56,47M in 1990AD, 67,8M in 2000AD and 85,66M by 2025AD. Following a decade of Balkan, Great War and Independence War attrition (1912-1922AD) and the 1923 Lausanne population exchange, Anatolia entered the Republican period under-populated and overwhelmingly agrarian. Post-war agricultural mechanisation, malaria eradication and sharp declines in infant mortality triggered rapid natural increase after 1950AD, while internal rural-to-urban migration shifted the demographic centre of gravity from the interior plateau toward the Marmara industrial corridor, Ankara, Izmir and the Mediterranean littoral. HANDBOOK harmonises 14 traditional Turkish general population censuses (1927-2000AD), the Address-Based Population Registration System (ADNKS, 2007-2024AD), seven late Ottoman vilayet aggregations (1881-1927AD), 968 modern second-level administrative districts (ilçes) and 326 coordinate-anchored settlement trajectories via strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic disaggregation across 11.653 5-arcminute grid cells. Across the urban cohort, aggregate inhabitants rose from 6,37M in 1923AD to 69,02M in 2025AD, exhibiting a steep Zipf rank-size slope of 1,1 ($R^2 = 0,98$) led by Istanbul (15,9M), Ankara (5,41M), Izmir (3,07M) and Bursa (2,14M). Over the last two decades, fertility has dropped below replacement even as Syrian refugee inflows after 2011AD added over 3M residents across southeastern border provinces and metropolitan Istanbul, leaving Turkey on the threshold of post-transitional demographic stabilisation.

# Background

Modern Turkish demography opens out of a severe demographic trough. On the eve of the First World War in 1914AD, the Ottoman vilayets corresponding roughly to the future Republican frontiers held roughly 14,17M inhabitants, distributed across a mixed Muslim, Greek Orthodox, Armenian and Syriac rural landscape [@Ustaoglu2021Reconstruc; @Hofmeester2020Shifting]. Ten consecutive years of mobilisation and conflict across the Balkan Wars (1912-1913AD), the Caucasian, Gallipoli and Mesopotamian campaigns (1914-1918AD), the wartime deportations and massacres of Anatolian Armenians, and the Greco-Turkish War (1919-1922AD) stripped Anatolia of roughly one-fifth of its pre-war numbers and destroyed urban commercial life across western and eastern provinces alike. The Treaty of Lausanne and its compulsory population exchange convention of January 1923 formalised a far-reaching ethnic and spatial reordering: roughly 1,2M Greek Orthodox Christians departed western Anatolia, Cappadocia and the Pontic coast for Greece, while between 380k and 500k Muslim refugees arrived from Macedonia, Thessaly, Epirus and Crete to resettle abandoned Aegean, Thracian and Black Sea farmlands [@Bakar2017Turkey; @Iflazoglu2025Rethinking]. At the foundation of the Republic in October 1923, the national population stood at 13,1M, climbing to 13,65M by the first systematic Republican enumeration in October 1927 [@Bostan2023Comparativ].

Throughout the single-party era (1923-1945AD), Republican policy treated demographic recovery as an existential priority. Pro-natalist legislation banned contraception, rewarded large families and promoted public-health campaigns against malaria, trachoma and tuberculosis across the river valleys of Cilicia, the Aegean and the Black Sea [@Bakar2017Turkey; @Furtuna2024Transition]. German and Central European agronomists advised state farms such as Tahirova on seed selection and pasture management, while railway construction linked Ankara, Sivas, Erzurum and Diyarbakir to the coast [@Hartmann2022Meeting; @Hartmann2023Planting]. At the same time, the state pursued cultural Turkification and resettlement policies that altered minority geographies. The 1937-1938AD military campaign in Dersim (modern Tunceli) killed tens of thousands of Kurdish Alevis and forcibly dispersed survivors across western Anatolian provinces [@Deniz2020Assessing; @Iflazoglu2025Rethinking]. Territorial annexation added the Sanjak of Alexandretta (Hatay province) in 1939AD, lifting the 1940AD census count to 17,82M despite the economic strain of Second World War mobilisation, which depressed marriages and births between 1940AD and 1945AD [@Bakar2017Turkey].

The decisive inflection arrived around 1950AD. Marshall Plan credits financed the rapid importation of tractors across the Konya Plain, Cukurova and Thrace, raising cultivated area while displacing sharecroppers and smallholders from the Anatolian interior [@Hartmann2022Meeting; @Karakoc2026Concentrat]. Simultaneously, antibiotics, DDT spraying and rural clinics cut crude death rates from above 25 per 1k in the 1930s to roughly 13 per 1k by the early 1960s while total fertility remained near 6 children per woman [@Bakar2017Turkey; @Furtuna2024Transition]. National population surged from 20,95M in 1950AD to 35,61M in 1970AD, generating annual growth rates approaching 2,8% and filling peripheral *gecekondu* (overnight-built) neighbourhoods around Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir [@Balc2022Istanbul; @Baysal2022Urbanizati].

From the early 1960s onward, state development plans managed surplus rural labour through bilateral labour recruitment agreements with West Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Belgium and France [@Klc2021Turkish; @Icduygu2012Turkey]. Although labour emigration drained hundreds of thousands of young men and women from central and northern Anatolia—establishing enduring Turkish diaspora communities whose nuptiality and fertility trajectories later diverged from their homeland peers [@Huschek2012Partner; @BaykaraKrumme2017Fertility]—remittances bolstered rural consumption while urban migration accelerated inside Turkey itself. Between 1970AD and 2000AD, the national total rose from 35,61M to 67,8M as export-oriented industrialisation expanded beyond Istanbul into Bursa, Kocaeli, Tekirdag, Gaziantep, Denizli, Kayseri and Konya [@Bostan2025Rkiye; @Oguz2021Resilient; @Cagatay2025Evolution]. In the east and southeast, high fertility combined with counter-insurgency evacuations during the 1980s and 1990s to drive Kurdish migration westward into Mersin, Adana, Antalya, Izmir and Istanbul [@Alptekin2024Three; @Canpolat2018Terms]. After 2007AD, Turkey replaced de facto decennial and quinquennial curfews with the continuous ADNKS civil register, recording 83,61M inhabitants in 2020AD and 85,66M by 2025AD—augmented after 2011AD by more than 3M Syrian nationals under temporary protection [@Bostan2023Comparativ; @INCILI2020Kilis; @BOLUKBASI2024Social].

# Methodology

## Census Regimes and Source Harmonisation

Reconstructing Turkish population from 1923AD to 2026AD bridges two distinct statistical architectures maintained by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TUIK) and its Republican predecessors. Between 1927AD and 2000AD, Turkey relied on traditional de facto general population censuses (*Genel Nüfus Sayımları*) conducted on a single Sunday under nationwide curfew: first in 1927AD, then quinquennially from 1935AD through 1990AD, and finally in October 2000 [@Bostan2023Comparativ; @Baysal2022Urbanizati]. Because municipal and provincial fiscal transfers depended on headcounts, local authorities occasionally contested or inflated urban totals in the 1990AD and 2000AD enumerations, a distortion rectified in November 2007 when Turkey inaugurated the *Adrese Dayalı Nüfus Kayıt Sistemi* (ADNKS), a continuous de jure population register linked to national identity numbers and municipal address databases [@Bostan2023Comparativ; @Bostan2025Rkiye].

To anchor the 1923AD independence baseline and smooth intercensal intervals, national totals follow TUIK's retrospective mid-year reconstructions from 1923AD to 1927AD, de facto census benchmarks at 1927AD, 1940AD, 1950AD, 1970AD, 1990AD and 2000AD, and annual ADNKS year-end cohorts through 2025AD. Provincial-level disaggregation tracks Turkey's contemporary 81-province (*il*) partition rather than freezing earlier 57-province or 67-province borders, preventing administrative splits—such as the elevation of Karaman (1989AD), Batman and Sirnak (1990AD), Bartin (1991AD), Igdir and Ardahan (1992AD), Yalova, Karabuk and Kilis (1995AD), Osmaniye (1996AD) and Duzce (1999AD)—from registering as artificial demographic drops in donor provinces [@Bostan2025Rkiye; @INCILI2020Kilis].

## Subadministrative GIS Disaggregation and Kriging Surface Coupling

Where historical and modern subadministrative tables exist below the national envelope, HANDBOOK integrates them through strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling over metric-isotropic radial distance fields and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging surfaces [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Two subadministrative layers govern the Turkish domain:

1. **Late Ottoman Vilayet Transition (1881–1927AD)**: Seven harmonised Ottoman provincial clusters derived from the 1881–1893AD and 1914AD Ottoman registers and linked directly to the 1927AD Republican provincial tally provide the pre-1923AD spatial prior across Eastern Anatolia, the Black Sea coast, Marmara-Thrace, the Aegean, northwestern Anatolia, north-central Anatolia and south-central Anatolia.
2. **Modern District Boundaries (ADM2, 1990–2023AD)**: Polygon geometries for 968 second-level districts (*ilçeler*) from geoBoundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] are rasterised onto the 5-arcminute global grid (4320 x 2160 resolution, covering 11.653 grid cells inside Turkey) and paired with district census series across 1990AD, 2000AD, 2009AD, 2011AD, 2013AD, 2017AD, 2022AD and 2023AD.

Within every administrative polygon $P_k$ at year $t$, pixel weights $w_i$ derived from biophysical habitability covariates (fluvial proximity, coastal access and terrain) and urban settlement masks are scaled multiplicatively so that $\sum_{i \in P_k} \hat{p}_{i,t} = P_{k,t}$ to machine precision. Across the entire HANDBOOK domain (29 historical and 2.645 modern subadministrative units over 83 disaggregated years), pycnophylactic auditing across 66.308 unit-year checks confirms 100% conservation within 0,01% and a global maximum unit relative error of 5,84e-08. Simultaneously, 326 coordinate-anchored urban settlements—screened against 331 candidate series after merging five subordinate suburbs within 2 km of primary municipal cores (Karasu, Sapanca, Saray, Kemer and Arakli)—capture metropolitan concentrations that coarse provincial areal weights alone would dilute.

# Testing and Validation

Validation across the Turkish reconstruction operates on three levels: cross-checking the 1927AD Republican census against late Ottoman vilayet sums, auditing subadministrative mass conservation across modern ADM2 districts, and comparing urban cohort trajectories against provincial totals and the 2012/2014 metropolitan municipal boundary reform.

First, summing the seven Ottoman vilayet blocks at 1927AD yields 13,65M (13.648.000 rounded), matching the 1927AD national total (13.648.001) within 0,01% and confirming that post-1923AD provincial boundaries preserve late Ottoman regional proportions once eastern depopulation (-40% across Erzurum, Van, Bitlis, Mamuretulaziz and Diyarbakir between 1914AD and 1927AD) and Aegean-Marmara refugee resettlement (+15,5% in Aydin vilayet) are accounted for [@Ustaoglu2021Reconstruc; @Bakar2017Turkey].

Second, inspecting the continuous 2010AD subadministrative surface (Figure \ref{fig:density-surface}) against the 81 provincial mask weights reveals an important structural property of the dataset. Because the provincial areal-mask table distributes national population across the 81 *il* polygons using areal-root spatial weighting (586 grid cells in Konya versus 70 in Istanbul), the areal-mask provincial series assigns Konya 2,25M and Sivas 1,9M in 2025AD while allocating only 795k to the Istanbul provincial polygon. Conversely, the 968 matched ADM2 *ilçe* polygons from geoBoundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] and the 326 settlement trajectories restore the true metropolitan concentration: in 2017AD, the 957 non-empty rasterised ADM2 units capture 84,6M inhabitants (99,5% of Turkey's registered population), led by Esenyurt (846,5k on 65 km²), Cankaya (922k), Kecioren (917,8k) and Osmangazi (856,8k).

Third, Turkey's Law No. 6360 (enacted in 2012AD and implemented at the March 2014 local elections) expanded metropolitan municipality (*büyükşehir belediyesi*) borders to provincial boundaries in 30 provinces, instantaneously reclassifying thousands of rural villages (*köy*) as urban neighbourhoods (*mahalle*) [@Canpolat2018Terms; @Bostan2025Rkiye]. As a result, official TUIK statistics jumped from roughly 77% urban in 2012AD to 91,3% in 2013AD and above 93% by 2023AD purely by legal redefinition. To prevent this administrative discontinuity from corrupting urban growth curves, HANDBOOK tracks continuous physical urban agglomerations across 1923-2025AD in the 326-settlement gazetteer (6,37M in 1923AD to 69,02M in 2025AD, or 80,6% functional urban share), keeping settlement series immune to municipal annexation artefacts [@Bostan2025Rkiye; @Oguz2021Resilient].

# Results

## National Demographic Trajectory and Transition Phases

Turkey's modern demographic expansion divides into four distinct regimes (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:national-series}). During the initial recovery phase (1923-1950AD), national population increased by 60%, from 13,1M to 20,95M, at an annualised rate of 1,76%. Growth was uneven across decades: after brisk post-exchange recovery between 1927AD and 1940AD (+4,17M, aided by Hatay's 1939AD accession), wartime mobilisation and food rationing slowed expansion between 1940AD and 1945AD before post-war health improvements revived natural increase [@Bakar2017Turkey; @Hartmann2022Meeting]. Mean population density across the 779.608 km² national territory rose from 16,8 inhabitants per km² in 1923AD to 26,9 per km² in 1950AD.

The second phase (1950-1980AD) marks Turkey's classic demographic explosion. As mortality plunged—driven by antibiotics, clean water systems and maternal clinics—while rural fertility declined only gradually from 6,9 births per woman in 1950AD to 4,3 in 1980AD, annual population growth accelerated above 2,5% [@Bakar2017Turkey; @Furtuna2024Transition]. Total numbers jumped by 14,66M between 1950AD and 1970AD (20,95M to 35,61M) and crossed 44,7M by 1980AD, even as roughly 800k contract workers departed for Western Europe under state labour accords [@Klc2021Turkish; @Icduygu2012Turkey].

During the third phase (1980-2007AD), fertility decline accelerated across western and central provinces under rising female schooling, urban wage employment and delayed marriage, lowering the national total fertility rate toward 2,2 by the mid-2000s [@Furtuna2024Transition; @Hatun2021Disentangl]. Yet population momentum kept absolute increments huge: Turkey added 20,87M people between 1970AD and 1990AD (35,61M to 56,47M) and another 11,33M in the single decade to 2000AD (67,8M).

In the contemporary ADNKS phase (2007-2026AD), domestic natural increase narrowed sharply as urban fertility dropped below 1,6 births per woman in the early 2020s, converging rapidly in western and central cities while remaining higher in southeastern provinces [@Hatun2021Disentangl; @BOLUKBASI2024Social]. National growth from 67,8M in 2000AD to 83,61M in 2020AD and 85,66M in 2025AD (109,9 inhabitants per km²) was sustained heavily by external inflows after 2011AD, when civil war in Syria pushed more than 3M refugees across the southern border into Kilis, Gaziantep, Hatay, Sanliurfa and Istanbul [@INCILI2020Kilis; @Klc2021Turkish]. By 2024AD, crude birth rates in coastal Marmara and Aegean provinces had fallen below crude death rates in ageing districts such as Sinop, Kastamonu and Edirne, placing Turkey on an ageing trajectory comparable to Southern Europe and Tunisia [@Bostan2023Comparativ; @BOLUKBASI2024Social].

## Late Ottoman Vilayet Continuity and 1927AD Realignment

Placing Republican censuses alongside the late Ottoman vilayet counts of 1881AD, 1893AD and 1914AD clarifies the geographic redistribution triggered by war and population exchange (Table \ref{tab:ottoman-bridge}). Across western and north-central Anatolia—specifically Aydin vilayet (Western Aegean, 1,72M in 1914AD to 1,99M in 1927AD), Hudavendigar (northwestern Anatolia, 1,62M to 1,8M), Konya and Adana (1,77M to 1,92M) and Ankara and Kastamonu (2,14M to 2,31M)—post-war Muslim refugee settlement from the Balkans and natural recovery fully offset wartime and Lausanne exchange losses by 1927AD [@Ustaoglu2021Reconstruc; @Bakar2017Turkey].

By contrast, the eastern vilayet group of Erzurum, Van, Bitlis, Mamuretulaziz (Elazig) and Diyarbakir suffered a catastrophic contraction of -40%, falling from 2,79M in 1914AD to 1,67M in 1927AD as Russian-Ottoman front warfare, famine, typhus and the eradication of the Ottoman Armenian population emptied rural districts across the Upper Euphrates and Lake Van basins. Similarly, Trabzon and Sivas declined from 2,6M to 2,45M (-5,8%) following Pontic Greek departures and front-line devastation, while Istanbul and Edirne slipped from 1,54M in 1914AD to 1,52M in 1927AD as the loss of imperial bureaucratic functions to Ankara and the departure of non-Muslim minorities offset incoming Thracian refugees [@Iflazoglu2025Rethinking; @Bakar2017Turkey].

## Provincial Areal Envelopes and 968 Modern Districts (ADM2)

Across the 81 modern provinces in the national areal mask, territorial weight correlates with provincial extent: Konya (40.249 km², 586 pixels) carries 2,25M in 2025AD, followed by Sivas (28.072 km², 1,9M), Ankara (25.603 km², 1,82M), Erzurum (23.758 km², 1,75M), Antalya (21.175 km², 1,62M), Sanliurfa (1,58M), Van (1,57M) and Kayseri (1,49M) (Table \ref{tab:top-provinces}). Because areal-mask disaggregation distributes the national curve evenly across spatial pixels before settlement-point sharpening, small coastal provinces such as Yalova (704 km², 11 pixels, 299,4k in the areal mask) exhibit the highest mask-level mean densities (367,9 per km² in Figure \ref{fig:density-surface}), followed by Kilis (276,4 per km²) and Bartin (216,2 per km²).

True sub-provincial demographic concentration becomes explicit only at the ADM2 (*ilçe*) level across the 968 matched geoBoundaries districts [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] (Table \ref{tab:adm2-top}). Between 2009AD and 2023AD, Turkey's most populous single district became Esenyurt on the European western fringe of Istanbul, surging by +142,1% from 403,9k to 978k within just 65 km² (15.046 inhabitants per km²) as mass residential construction absorbed Anatolian migrants, working-class families pushed out of inner Bosporus wards and Syrian newcomers. Across greater Istanbul, neighbouring outer districts such as Kucukcekmece (674,8k to 792k on 62 km²), Pendik (562,1k to 743,8k) and Umraniye (573,3k to 723,8k) recorded comparable gains while older historic peninsular districts stagnated or lost residents to commercial conversion.

In southeastern Anatolia, Gaziantep's twin metropolitan districts of Sahinbey (722k to 939,5k, +30,1%) and Sehitkamil (602,3k to 867,2k, +44%) expanded rapidly on the strength of export textile manufacturing and border logistics [@Oguz2021Resilient; @Cagatay2025Evolution]. In the capital, Cankaya (937,5k), Kecioren (923,4k) and Yenimahalle (701,6k) anchored Ankara's multi-node metropolitan basin, while Osmangazi in Bursa reached 885,3k (+15,6%), Seyhan in Adana stood at 787,8k and Selcuklu in Konya climbed from 487,9k to 695,8k (+42,6%).

At the opposite end of the ADM2 distribution, remote interior highland and border districts hollowed out steadily over the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. In the 2023AD subadministrative roster, Yalihuyuk in Konya (1,85k), Kiziloren in Afyonkarahisar (2,11k), Yayladere in Bingol (2,3k), Kofcaz in Kirklareli (2,31k) and Han in Eskisehir (2,35k) held fewer than 2,5k inhabitants each across hundreds of square kilometres [@Canpolat2018Terms; @Duman2025Organize]. This bifurcation between hyper-dense Marmara-Anatolian corridors and depopulating rural *ilçes* aligns with provincial GDP clustering studies showing persistent productivity divergence favouring Istanbul, Kocaeli, Tekirdag, Ankara, Izmir and Bursa over northeastern and eastern highland provinces [@Baysal2022Urbanizati; @Karakoc2026Concentrat; @Bostan2025Rkiye; @UNAL2025Interactio].

## Urban Polarisation and Rank-Size Structure

Across the 326 catalogued urban agglomerations (Figure \ref{fig:settlements-zipf} and Table \ref{tab:top-settlements}), aggregate urban numbers grew tenfold from 6,37M in 1923AD to 69,02M in 2025AD, elevating the functional urban share from 48,6% to 80,6%. Unlike Egypt's extreme Nile primate dominance, Turkey developed a multi-polar urban backbone anchored in the western industrial crescent (Istanbul, Bursa, Gebze, Izmit, Adapazari, Corlu, Tekirdag), the Aegean port and agricultural valley complex (Izmir, Denizli, Manisa, Aydin, Torbali, Menemen), the central plateau administrative-industrial axis (Ankara, Konya, Kayseri, Eskisehir), and the Cilician-Upper Mesopotamian southern arc (Adana, Mersin, Gaziantep, Sanliurfa, Diyarbakir, Antakya, Kahramanmaras).

Istanbul alone grew more than elevenfold (11,36x) from 1,4M in 1923AD to 15,9M in 2025AD, absorbing waves of Black Sea, Central Anatolian and Kurdish migrants into sprawling outer districts while driving peri-urban forest conversion and ecological stress across the northern Bosporus and Thracian hinterlands [@Balc2022Istanbul; @KOSE2022Impact; @Bostan2025Rkiye]. Ankara multiplied 9,47x from 571,4k to 5,41M, reshaping the steppe ecology of the Golbasi flats and surrounding valleys [@Dolcerocca2024Restoratio]. Yet the highest relative growth rates belonged to industrial satellites and Mediterranean tourism-horticulture hubs: Torbali near Izmir expanded 42,5x (4,8k to 205,8k), Gursu near Bursa 35,7x (2,9k to 104,2k), Gebze in the Kocaeli industrial belt 33,9x (23,7k to 801,4k), Silivri west of Istanbul 33,6x (6k to 200,1k), Karakopru outside Sanliurfa 33,4x (7,5k to 251,9k), and Antalya 20,7x (66,8k to 1,38M) alongside Alanya (26,9x) and Bodrum (25,7x) [@DEMIR2022Antalya; @Alptekin2024Three]. By contrast, older coal-mining Zonguldak grew only 3,52x (30,1k to 106,1k), confronting post-industrial brownfield contraction after the 1980s [@Ergen2013Methodolog]. Across all 326 settlements in 2025AD, the rank-size regression returns a Zipf exponent of $\alpha = 1,10$ ($R^2 = 0,98$), confirming an integrated national urban hierarchy slightly steeper than strict unitary Zipf scaling owing to Istanbul's commercial primacy.

## Fertility Convergence, International Migration and Border Shocks

Regional demographic divergence inside modern Turkey rests equally on uneven fertility decline and cross-border population movements. While Istanbul, Izmir and Thrace crossed below replacement fertility in the 1990s, provinces across Southeastern and Eastern Anatolia maintained total fertility rates above 3,5 children per woman into the 2000s before rapid female schooling and urbanisation compressed eastern fertility toward 2,3-2,6 by the early 2020s [@Hatun2021Disentangl; @Bostan2023Comparativ]. Multivariate analyses of Turkish Demographic and Health Survey waves demonstrate that secularisation, delayed age at marriage and urban labour-market participation explain most of the timing gap between western metropolitan cores and interior highlands, while migrant cohorts settling in western European cities converged rapidly toward host-country family sizes across the second generation [@Furtuna2024Transition; @BaykaraKrumme2017Fertility; @Huschek2012Partner].

After 2011AD, Turkey transitioned from a net emigrant country to the world's largest host of displaced persons, absorbing over 3,1M to 3,6M Syrian nationals under temporary protection alongside smaller Afghan, Iraqi and Iranian inflows [@Klc2021Turkish; @INCILI2020Kilis]. In border Kilis, registered Syrian arrivals briefly approached or exceeded the local Turkish municipal population, transforming retail, housing and infrastructure across southern border towns before secondary internal mobility shifted hundreds of thousands toward Gaziantep, Adana, Mersin, Bursa and Istanbul [@INCILI2020Kilis; @Bostan2025Rkiye]. Concurrently, rural crime, forest encroachment along expanding Thracian commuter belts and seismic vulnerability—demonstrated by the 1999AD Marmara and February 2023 Kahramanmaras earthquakes—continue to reshape settlement policy and metropolitan growth boundaries [@UNAL2025Interactio; @Duman2025Organize; @Oguz2021Resilient].

## Seven Geographical Regions and Spatial Contrasts

Viewed across Turkey's seven standard geographical regions, century-long demographic change reflects a sustained westward and coastal shift punctuated by southeastern natural increase.

In the Marmara region—comprising Istanbul, Kocaeli, Bursa, Tekirdag, Sakarya, Balikesir, Canakkale, Edirne, Kirklareli, Bilecik and Yalova—post-1950AD manufacturing concentrated nearly one-third of Turkey's urban population into a continuous metropolitan belt along the Sea of Marmara [@Bostan2025Rkiye; @Ustaoglu2021Reconstruc]. Industrial spillover turned former agricultural market towns in Tekirdag (Corlu, Cerkezkoy) and Kocaeli (Gebze, Darica, Cayirova) into major manufacturing centres, placing mounting pressure on northern Thracian and Bithynian woodlands [@UNAL2025Interactio; @KOSE2022Impact].

Along the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts, Izmir, Denizli, Aydin, Manisa, Antalya, Mersin and Adana combined irrigated export agriculture (cotton, citrus, figs and greenhouse horticulture) with port logistics and mass coastal tourism [@DEMIR2022Antalya; @Oguz2021Resilient]. Antalya's provincial urban core expanded more than twentyfold after 1923AD as highway construction, greenhouse farming and seasonal service employment drew migrants from both Central Anatolia and the Kurdish east [@DEMIR2022Antalya; @Alptekin2024Three].

Across Central Anatolia and the Black Sea coast, trajectories diverged sharply between state-anchored urban corridors and rural highlands. Ankara, Eskisehir, Konya and Kayseri absorbed provincial migrants into public administration, defence industries, universities and Anatolian small-and-medium enterprises [@Karakoc2026Concentrat; @Dolcerocca2024Restoratio]. By contrast, mountain provinces of the eastern and western Black Sea—Artvin, Gumushane, Bayburt, Sinop, Kastamonu and Bartin—and interior plateau provinces such as Yozgat, Corum, Sivas and Cankiri experienced decades of net out-migration toward Istanbul and Ankara [@Baysal2022Urbanizati; @Canpolat2018Terms].

In Eastern and Southeastern Anatolia, high fertility sustained rapid population growth into the 1990s despite persistent out-migration. Diyarbakir, Sanliurfa, Gaziantep and Van swelled into regional metropolises exceeding half a million to nearly two million residents each as rural mechanisation, irrigation expansion under the Southeastern Anatolia Project (GAP), security displacements during the 1990s and post-2011AD cross-border inflows concentrated rural populations into provincial capitals [@Alptekin2024Three; @INCILI2020Kilis].

# Limitations

Four methodological and evidentiary constraints qualify these figures. First, the 81-province areal-mask table allocates national totals across provinces proportionally to grid-cell extent rather than observed provincial census totals, which exaggerates spacious interior provinces (Konya, Sivas, Erzurum) relative to compact metropolitan Istanbul (70 cells); sub-provincial spatial accuracy therefore depends on pairing the provincial mask with the 968 geoBoundaries ADM2 units [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] and the 326 settlement coordinates. Second, ADM2 coverage varies across years (957 non-empty rasterised districts in 2017AD capturing 84,6M, versus partial district matches in 1990AD, 2000AD and 2022AD), requiring caution when comparing raw ADM2 sums across non-uniform sample years. Third, the transition from de facto curfew enumerations (1927-2000AD) to de jure ADNKS address registration (2007-2025AD) shifted student, conscript and seasonal worker allocations across provincial borders [@Bostan2023Comparativ]. Fourth, post-2011AD Syrian refugees under temporary protection—numbering over 3,1M across Turkey in 2023-2025AD, with acute local concentrations in Kilis, Hatay, Gaziantep, Sanliurfa and Istanbul—are recorded in separate Migration Management Directorate registries rather than standard citizen ADNKS counts, creating under-registration in border *ilçes* unless explicitly reconciled [@INCILI2020Kilis; @Klc2021Turkish]. Additionally, the February 2023 Kahramanmaras earthquakes displaced more than 2M residents out of eleven southeastern provinces, introducing rapid short-term shifts in local district occupancy not yet fully stabilised in permanent address rolls.

# Conclusion

Between 1923AD and 2026AD, Turkey executed one of the fastest demographic and spatial transformations in the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, expanding from 13,1M sparsely settled post-war survivors to 85,66M predominantly urban inhabitants. Pro-natalist interwar recovery gave way after 1950AD to falling mortality, agricultural mechanisation and sustained internal migration toward Marmara, Ankara, the Aegean and Cukurova, lifting the 326-city urban cohort from 6,37M (1923AD) to 69,02M (2025AD) along a well-behaved Zipf distribution ($\alpha = 1,10$, $R^2 = 0,98$). By combining late Ottoman vilayet bridges (1881-1927AD), TUIK censuses (1927-2000AD), ADNKS registers (2007-2025AD), 968 modern ADM2 district polygons disaggregated with mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling, and 326 continuous urban trajectories, HANDBOOK resolves both the national vital transition and the sub-provincial polarisations reshaping contemporary Anatolia and Thrace.

# Appendix

Four settlements in the 326-city Turkish gazetteer carry explicit post-1923AD or nineteenth-century industrial foundation benchmarks: Zonguldak (1849AD coal port, 30,1k in 1923AD to 106,1k in 2025AD), Kirikkale (1925AD state munitions complex, reaching 195k), Karabuk (1937AD iron and steel works, reaching 130,8k) and Batman (1940AD petroleum discovery, surging to 481,1k by 2025AD) (Table \ref{tab:industrial-foundations}). Five minor satellite towns located within 2 km of primary urban cores (Karasu, Sapanca, Saray, Kemer and Arakli) were merged into their parent municipal trajectories during candidate screening, yielding 326 included settlement series out of 331 evaluated entries.
